items.title: Would you pay to have the ‘best baby’? Liberal eugenics and the troubling quest for human perfection
The Berlin Airlift
items.content:
In 1948, the ruins of Berlin became the first major battleground of the Cold War. Encircled behind the Iron Curtain, the German capital faced a brutal choice: submit to Stalin’s blockade, or freeze and starve. And with trigger-happy generals eyeing their atomic weapons, the Western Allies launched a humanitarian gamble that many condemned as utter madness.

Dan Snow is joined by Joseph Pearson, author of 'The Airlift', to unpack the dramatic tale of the Berlin Airlift - from the story of an American pilot who once dropped bombs on Berlin, to that of a little girl who was upset that the older boys kept stealing her chocolate.

Produced by James Hickmann and edited by Dougal Patmore.

items.title: 725. The Death of Captain Cook: At World’s End (Part 1)
The Neolithic Revolution
items.content:
What is the greatest revolution in human history? Unlike the invention of the steam engine, the rise of states or the birth of modern industry, the answer HAS to be the moment humanity stopped hunting and gathering and started farming. Known as the Neolithic Revolution, it transformed how humans lived, laying the foundations for the first settlements, towns and eventually empires.

Today, Tristan Hughes is joined by Luke Kemp to explore this extraordinary turning point in human history. Why did people begin to cultivate crops and domesticate animals? How did farming transform human societies? And how did this revolution set humanity on the path towards the world we know today?

items.title: Akhenaten and Nefertiti (Radio Edit)
items.content:
Greg Jenner is joined in ancient Egypt by historian and curator Dr Campbell Price and comedian Sikisa to learn all about Tutankhamun’s parents, Nefertiti and Akhenaten.

As well as their famous son, this ancient Egyptian power couple are best known in the modern age for two reasons. Firstly, Nefertiti’s legendary beauty – her portrait bust is instantly recognisable around the world. Secondly, Akhenaten’s religious radicalism, which saw him reorient Egyptian belief towards the sun god Aten and build an entirely new capital away from the traditional seat of power at Thebes.

This episode traces their lives as members of the 18th dynasty, often regarded as the ‘Golden Age’ of pharaonic Egypt. We look at Akhenaten’s murky childhood and Nefertiti’s even murkier origins, exploring their family life and the children they had, the religious revolution that Akhenaten drove, the unique architecture and art styles developed during their reign, and the fate of Aten worship after Akhenaten’s death. Along the way, we dig into the archaeological evidence and the many uncertainties surrounding their lives, and ask whether they really were Tutankhamun’s parents after all.

This is a radio edit of the original podcast episode. For the full-length version, please look further back in the feed.

, creator of Superpowers and founder of Prime Radiant, joins us to explore what it actually takes to get useful work out of AI agents.

items.title: The Rise of the Software Factories
items.content:
AI coding agents have made individual developers dramatically more productive, yet most organizations aren’t seeing anything close to that gain at the company level. A key reason is that shipping a feature to production involves far more than writing code. Triage, review, context, guardrails, and human approvals all surround the work, and agents add new risk by acting in ways teams can’t always see or control. Turning individual gains into real organizational throughput, has become one of the central challenges of the agentic era.

Port is an AI software factory platform that lets platform engineers build, operate, and govern an AI software factory which is a layer that sits above the coding agents. The factory is model and agent agnostic while supplying a context lake that encodes an organization’s taxonomy and data, governance, and guardrails across each stage of the software lifecycle, human-in-the-loop checkpoints, orchestration across different agents, and a registry of approved agents and skills.

Yonatan Boguslavski is the CTO and a co-founder at Port. In this episode, he joins Kevin Ball to talk about the shift from writing features to “factory engineering,” how a context lake structures organizational knowledge so agents can actually use it, how governance works across an agentic software lifecycle, and the build-versus-buy question of where a platform like Port fits.Full Disclosure: This episode is sponsored by Portsponsor@softwareengineeringdaily.com

items.title: Hatshepsut: Was This Really Egypt's Greatest Pharaoh?
items.content:
What does it take to be a great ruler? Rameses II, Akhenaten, Seti I- the great Egyptian Pharaohs- would have you believe it's building towering monoliths and waging great wars. But shouldn't it be someone who maintains peace, manages diplomacy to create a flourishing and healthy civilisation?

This is something the Pharaoh Hatshepsut was extraordinarily good at. In the 18th dynasty, she oversaw one of the most prosperous times in Ancient Egyptian history, expanded its influence further and made its people richer than ever before. Joining Dan to argue her case is Dr Campbell Price, curator of Egypt and Sudan at Manchester Museum.

items.title: From the archive: Dark waters: how the adventure of a lifetime turned to tragedy
The Technical Interview Is Broken
items.content:
The technical interview has long been used as a proxy for actual job performance. Brain teasers, data structure puzzles, or reversing a linked list became the price of admission to employment as a developer in many organizations, even though few engineers do that work day to day. It would seem AI has now broken that model entirely, since an LLM can one-shot any classic algorithm question. This is forcing tech companies to rethink what an interview should measure.

Vivek Ravisankar is the co-founder and CEO of HackerRank, which is one of the most well-known platforms for tech interview practice problems. In this episode, Vivek joins Josh Goldberg to discuss why old-style interviews stopped working, the company’s “apology tour” for years of algorithm puzzles, how to keep AI evaluation fair and trustworthy, and where both models and the shape of hiring may be headed as software engineering becomes something every role does.sponsor@softwareengineeringdaily.com

items.title: Multi-Cloud LLM Routing and Context-Aware Coding Agents
items.author: Demetrios
items.content:
In this episode, we sit down with and , engineers at Cloudflare and Miro, to look at how two very different companies are building their own AI software factories, and what happens to engineering when the code mostly writes and reviews itself.

We start with the AI gateway: why a model call is no longer simple when the same model is served across multiple regions, multiple clouds, and direct from the provider, and how Miro pools rate limits and data residency rules (like EU-only models for German customers) into a single routing layer that also powers Miro’s Sidekicks. Matt walks through Cloudflare’s agent stack, from the AI gateway and Agents SDK to Flue, a JavaScript agent framework from the makers of Astro, and Cloudflare OS, an open source agent office suite he even runs at home for grocery shopping.

The heart of the conversation is code review. Matt describes what he calls the best AI code reviewer he’s ever used, built on Flue and powered by an internal engineering codex written only for agents. Scott breaks down Miro’s three-layer setup, including Easel, a bot that reads production logs overnight and opens fix PRs before anyone wakes up, and explains why only about half of those PRs get merged, and how that signal is fed back to teach the system what people care about.

Along the way, we cover agent experience as a new discipline, how open source maintainers are handling a flood of cheap AI pull requests, Astro reaching zero open issues, when companies should open source internal tools and how to retire them gracefully, plus a few hot takes on chocolate and nuts. We close on the rise of the “scholarly engineer,” and why understanding ideas may matter more than reading every line of code.

items.title: Anne Bonny and Mary Read (Radio Edit)
items.content:
Greg Jenner is joined in the 18th-century Caribbean by historian and curator Hannah Cusworth and comedian Kemah Bob to learn about the swashbuckling lives of pirates Anne Bonny and Mary Read. These women and their adventures on the high seas have become the stuff of legend, helped along by the sensational account of their lives written shortly after their capture.

Though they are famous for the short period they spent together on a pirate ship, dressed as men to hide their true identities, the two had very different backgrounds. Anne was the well-off and rebellious daughter of a merchant and plantation owner in Carolina, while the working-class Mary already had experience dressing in men’s clothing and working as a sailor and soldier.

This episode traces their biographies, exploring their upbringings, romantic entanglements (with men and each other), and time aboard the pirate ship captained by the infamous Captain 'Calico Jack' Rackham, as well as their ultimate fate. And it looks at the wider context of the Caribbean, the transatlantic trade in enslaved Africans and the Golden Age of piracy which shaped their lives and choices, and asks what place they have in queer and trans histories of the period.

This is a radio edit of the original podcast episode. For the full-length version, please look further back in the feed.

items.title: Fraud Prevention in the Age of AI Agents
items.content:
A major challenge for almost every online service is reliably identifying users, and knowing whether a given user or agent can be trusted. Historically, web services leaned on cookies stored in the browser to remember a visitor and recognize them when they return. The problem is that cookies live in the user’s own browser and are easy to remove, block, or avoid entirely, so a bad actor can simply clear them to escape recognition. IP blocking and CAPTCHA puzzles are firmer approaches, but they can frustrate legitimate users while doing little to stop a determined attacker. That leaves developers stuck between being too lax and losing control, or too strict and driving real users away.

FingerprintJS was started in 2012 as an open-source project. In 2019, Fingerprint was launched as a separate, full commercial platform, built on the original FingerprintJS GitHub library, to recognize devices and browsers without relying on cookies. It handles identification by reading over 100 signals, from fonts and screen resolution to how a device renders audio and graphics.

Keshia Rose works in Developer Relations at Fingerprint. In this episode she joins Gregor Vand to talk about fingerprinting, how Fingerprint combines multiple signals to identify fraudulent actors, how to distinguish legitimate AI agent use from anonymous or malicious bots, and how Fingerprint’s research team uncovered and disclosed a privacy vulnerability in Firefox and Tor that could have been used to track people across the web.Full Disclosure: This episode is sponsored by Fingerprint

items.title: GitLab and the Evolution of DevSecOps
items.content:
AI coding agents can already reach well beyond the code in front of them. Through connections to tools like Slack, Jira, and Sentry, an agent can pull in issues, discussions, and production signals from across an organization. However, that context is scattered across many separate systems, with no shared map of how it all connects and no common controls over what an agent is allowed to touch. For a large enterprise, stitching that together while staying compliant, auditable, and sometimes fully cut off from the internet is a hard problem.

GitLab runs one of the major platforms where software gets built, hosted, and shipped. That gives it a wide view of everything around the code, which shapes how it is approaching the agent era. The bet is that AI is most useful when it can draw on the full context of a project and stay under enterprise control, rather than acting as a point tool bolted onto a single repository. Getting there means wrestling with hard questions about governance, agent identity, and how much autonomy to hand over.

Tim Zallmann is the VP of Engineering at GitLab. In this episode, he joins Gregor Vand to discuss bringing AI to the full software development lifecycle, why running agents under enterprise control matters for governance and auditing, how to track which human is behind an agent’s actions, the realities of shipping air-gapped software, and how the space is shifting as new players move into code hosting.

items.title: My AI Agent Bought Me A Car
items.author: Demetrios
items.content:
’s first real test of Hermes Agent was a shopping tool that matched clothes to photos of ancient pottery. A few months later, the same agent was checking government auction sites every day until it found him a retired three-wheel parking ticket car, which he now drives around San Francisco. In this episode, recorded at AGNTCon + MCPCon North America in San Jose, Sam, who works on the RL post-training team at Nous Research, goes from those everyday wins to the question everyone in AI is asking: can agents improve themselves?

He explains how Hermes grew from an internal productivity tool into one of the most talked-about open-source agents, and why letting it write its own skills was the moment it clicked for users. He also describes an early version that could design its own RL environment, train on Thinking Machines’ Tinker, and hot-swap the new weights into a model running locally. Sam then breaks down Trace to Environment, an idea he credits to Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.6-Pro work, and the loop Nous is building around it: find the exact point where an agent fails, cluster those failures by type, synthesize environments that recreate them, and train on them again and again.

The second half moves from training to inference. We get into whether reasoning models overthink, why leaning on pretraining knowledge can be a model’s Achilles heel, and why choosing a reasoning effort level may be a temporary quirk. Sam also makes his case for activation steering as an underexplored way to get more out of small models, explains where steering meets interpretability, and describes what true continual learning could look like.

items.title: Everyone hates Oxford Street. Will pedestrianisation save it?
A Deep Dive on Submarines
items.content:
For centuries, humans have been fascinated by the mysteries of the deep sea. The history of submarines is one of extraordinary invention, daring exploration and deadly warfare. From the first experimental underwater vessels of the 17th century to the devastating U-boats of the First and Second World Wars, submarines have transformed naval warfare and revolutionised our understanding of the oceans.

Today, Dan visits the Royal Navy Submarine Museum in Gosport and is joined by curator Alexandra Geary to discover the eccentric origins of underwater travel and the dramatic submarine battles of WWI and WWII in honour of the 125th anniversary of the Royal Navy Submarine Service. He also speaks to Vice Admiral Sir Tim McClement, who was Second in Command on HMS Conqueror during the sinking of the Argentine ARA General Belgrano warship in the Falklands, as well as First Sea Lord General Sir Gwyn Jenkins on how AI might shape the submarines of the future.

With huge thanks to Commander James 'Dally' Dalrymple and Annarose Hearsum.

items.title: Medieval Saints (Radio Edit)
items.content:
Greg Jenner is joined in medieval Europe by historian Dr Simon Yarrow and comedian Rachel Parris to learn all about the cult of saints and their relics. The veneration of saints still plays an important role in the lives of Catholics all over the world, but what did the cult of saints – and especially devotion to their relics – play in medieval Europe?

This episode explores all aspects of the topic: who became a saint, and how the canonisation process changed over the centuries as the papacy tried to more tightly control it. What sorts of signs and miracles proved someone’s sanctity. What relics are, and how medieval churches acquired them, both legitimately and illegitimately. What people in the Middle Ages thought saints could do for them, and the pilgrimages they took to their tombs in search of aid. And it asks whether everyone believed in the power of saints’ relics – and the gruesome fate awaiting some sceptics.

This is a radio edit of the original podcast episode. For the full-length version, please look further back in the feed.

items.title: ‘The last bastion is gone’: the US right idolised Orbán’s Hungary. Can they recover now he has fallen?
Cut One AI Cost and Two More Grow Back
items.author: Demetrios
items.content:
What does AI really cost once thousands of people inside a company start using it? , Director of AI at Prosus, has been running agents in production since 2024. We put that question to him on a tandem bike ride from a favorite Amsterdam cafe to Vondelpark.

Ioannis explains the decision to stop relying purely on cloud APIs, and why that approach breaks down at the scale of a large company. He covers why agent harnesses and sandboxes are as greedy as software gets, and why agents scheduled to run every five minutes repeat a lesson the data world already learned about freshness. He also explains how the habit of throwing away a codebase and prompting again quietly adds up. His bigger point is that even if model progress froze tomorrow, there would still be about two years of value left to squeeze out. The cheapest wins come from controlling context and running a basic model router, while ten new features a month keep sprouting like Hydra heads.

From there we get into when fine-tuning small models pays off for repetitive work like data analytics, and the eval suites that come as a byproduct of building in-house. Ioannis explains how owning the stack let Prosus grow a GPT-3 Slack bot into a full agent harness. He also explains why committing to a single vendor or open source project is a bigger bet than it looks, and how to balance top-down priorities with bottom-up building across the company. We close on hiring. Ioannis looks for system design over syntax, a nose for the over-engineered code AI models love to produce, and enough agent intuition to know when to build something yourself and when to let the agent decide.

items.title: SED News: PHP’s Megabug, a Hidden Mic at OpenAI, and Dead AI Products
items.content:
SED News is a monthly podcast from Software Engineering Daily where hosts Gregor Vand and Sean Falconer break down the biggest stories shaping software engineering, Silicon Valley, and the broader tech industry.

In this episode, Gregor and Sean cover the PHP remote code execution flaw that hit an estimated 70 percent of the internet, the recording device an OpenAI employee hid in a conference room, and a busy run of deals including Chroma joining Replit, Cloudflare taking Deno, and Supabase acquiring Turso.

The main topic tours the AI graveyard, sorting recent product failures into patterns: features swallowed by bigger platforms, runaway hits too costly or risky to sustain, interfaces made redundant by agents, and hardware that never materialized.

As always, the episode wraps up with a few standout Hacker News threads, including why washing machines took 50 years to catch on, a location-aware local Wikipedia, and a Figma quirk that traces back to the Windows Numlock key.sponsor@softwareengineeringdaily.com

WWI's Stalingrad: The Siege of Przemyśl
items.content:
Bread cut with sawdust. Horses boiled to the bone. Men trading pet dogs and mice for scraps.

In the brutal winter of 1914 to 1915, the grand Austro-Hungarian fortress of Przemyśl came under siege. Cut off by Russian armies and doomed by the vanity of their own generals, the garrison survived by the skin of their teeth until a final, desperate breakout charge…

Dan Snow is joined by Alexander Watson, author of ‘The Fortress’, to step inside WWI’s longest, bloodiest siege.

items.title: We now have Kerr’s Law (Interview)
items.content:
Dave Kerr created hacker laws, and now he finds himself reviewing agent-written code for them. Back on the show after six years, Dave names what he sees limiting teams today: keeping everyone’s mental model in sync with what’s actually been built. Adam declares it Kerr’s Law on the spot. We get into why Dave’s team treats code review as a deliberate slowdown, how Shellwright lets agents bring evidence to a pull request, and what living with bipolar disorder has taught Dave about noticing when the excitement of these tools stops being healthy.
